summary: Defines a protocol that tunnels DTLS traffic in multimedia conferences so a Media Distributor can help an endpoint and the Key Distributor do key exchange. The Media Distributor gets the keys for hop-by-hop protection, but not the keys for end-to-end protection. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A middleman helps pass notes between friends and the key keeper, but can only open the outer envelope, not the inner one.

questions: how to protect media from intermediaries
subtitle: A protocol for secure key exchange in multimedia conferences with selective transparency.

tldr.problem: In multimedia conferences with a central Media Distributor, the distributor needs access to hop-by-hop encryption keys to process media, but should never see the end-to-end keys between endpoints, creating a key exchange problem.
tldr.mechanism: A TLS tunnel is established between the Media Distributor and a Key Distributor. Endpoints perform DTLS-SRTP key negotiation with the Key Distributor, with DTLS messages forwarded through the Media Distributor. The Key Distributor then shares only the hop-by-hop keys with the Media Distributor.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints gain end-to-end encryption that is invisible to the Media Distributor, while the Media Distributor can process and protect media with hop-by-hop encryption. This enables Privacy-Enhanced RTP Conferencing (PERC).

today: RFC 9185 is an Informational specification from April 2022 that defines a tunneling protocol for Privacy-Enhanced RTP Conferencing. The specification is aligned with the PERC framework and related security RFCs on double encryption.

sections.title: Secure Conferencing with a Middleman
sections.content:
Privacy-Enhanced RTP Conferencing (PERC) aims to allow endpoints in a multimedia conference to encrypt media while a central Media Distributor (e.g., a conference bridge) processes the encrypted streams. The challenge is that the Media Distributor needs encryption keys to verify and forward media packets, but must not see the keys protecting communication between endpoints.

This document specifies a tunneling protocol that enables endpoints to establish a secure key exchange with a Key Distributor (a trusted key management server) while the Media Distributor acts as a relay. The result is double encryption: one layer that the Media Distributor can decrypt and work with (hop-by-hop), and another layer that remains secret from the Media Distributor (end-to-end).
sections.plainLanguage: In a big conference call, a middleman forwards all the audio and video, and needs to be able to work with it, but the calls should also be secret from the middleman. This memo explains how to give the middleman access to one layer of secrecy but not another.

sections.title: The Tunneling Architecture
sections.content:
The protocol establishes a secure TLS connection (a tunnel) between the Media Distributor and the Key Distributor. This tunnel remains open and is used to relay DTLS messages between many endpoints and the Key Distributor. When an endpoint wants to establish an encrypted media session, it performs a DTLS-SRTP handshake as if speaking directly to the Key Distributor, but the DTLS messages are transparently forwarded through the Media Distributor via the tunnel.

The tunnel itself uses TLS and is mutually authenticated, meaning the Media Distributor and Key Distributor verify each other's identity. A single tunnel can relay messages for multiple endpoint-to-Key-Distributor associations simultaneously, making the protocol scalable.
sections.plainLanguage: The Media Distributor opens a secret phone line to the Key Distributor. Endpoints send their keys over this line without the Media Distributor seeing them, but the Media Distributor gets a copy of the outer key it needs.

sections.title: Message Flow and Key Exchange
sections.content:
When a tunnel is established, the Media Distributor first sends a SupportedProfiles message listing the SRTP protection profiles (encryption algorithms) it can handle. The endpoint then initiates a DTLS handshake toward the Key Distributor, sending DTLS handshake messages through the Media Distributor inside TunneledDtls messages.

The Key Distributor extracts the DTLS messages and processes them as if the endpoint connected directly. Once the DTLS handshake completes, the endpoint and Key Distributor have agreed on encryption keys. The Key Distributor then sends a MediaKeys message to the Media Distributor containing only the hop-by-hop (HBH) keys and the selected cipher, excluding the end-to-end (E2E) keys. The E2E keys go only to the endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: First, everyone agrees on what encryption methods work. Then the endpoint and key keeper shake hands to agree on secret keys. The key keeper gives the middleman a copy of the outer key, but keeps the inner key secret.

sections.title: Roles and Responsibilities
sections.content:
The endpoint follows standard DTLS-SRTP procedures, unaware that its messages are being tunneled. It must include a unique session identifier in both the SDP offer (the tls-id attribute) and the DTLS ClientHello message to prevent key confusion attacks.

The Media Distributor assigns a unique identifier (a UUID) for each endpoint's DTLS association and includes it in all messages. It forwards all DTLS messages between the endpoint and Key Distributor transparently, and extracts the HBH keys from the MediaKeys message to use for processing media.

The Key Distributor acts as a DTLS server, matching the endpoint's session identifier with the tls-id received via SDP to ensure keys go to the right conference. It selects an encryption algorithm supported by the endpoint, Media Distributor, and itself, then shares HBH keys with the Media Distributor while keeping E2E keys secret from it.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoint doesn't know it's being relayed; it just talks to the key keeper. The middleman keeps track of who is who and passes messages along. The key keeper makes sure the right key goes to the right person and only gives the middleman what it needs.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
The protocol relies on TLS for transport security and on DTLS-SRTP for establishing encryption keys. The mutual authentication of the TLS tunnel between Media Distributor and Key Distributor ensures that only authorized distributors can access HBH keys. Without this, a rogue distributor could forge HBH-authenticated packets and disrupt the conference.

E2E keys remain secret from the Media Distributor throughout. The protocol does not prevent a compromised Media Distributor from discarding media or replaying old packets, but it prevents the distributor from decrypting or forging E2E-protected content. The use of unique identifiers tied to SDP prevents a malicious Media Distributor from misdirecting keys between endpoints.

Implementations must guard against unsolicited DTLS messages that could consume resources on the Media Distributor and Key Distributor. The protocol defines an EndpointDisconnect message to clean up state when an endpoint leaves, preventing resource exhaustion.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret line between middleman and key keeper can't be tapped. The key keeper is the only one who knows the inner secrets. The middleman can't forge the inner messages or trick them into the wrong conference. If the middleman goes bad, it can't read or make up the inner secrets.
